main_damage_causes: Omission of Aberforth's central monologue about Ariana removes the emotional and moral core of his characterisation, leaving him as a bitter cynic without the specific grief, love, and backstory that justify his position.

Reversal of the Ariana–Aberforth bond (attributing her devotion to Albus rather than Aberforth) dismantles the relational logic underpinning his estrangement from his brother and his personal stake in the events of the saga.

Removal of Aberforth's active confrontation of Grindelwald as a teenager and his participation in the Battle of Hogwarts strips him of moral agency at both the backstory and climactic levels, reducing a character defined by inarticulate but real courage to a purely reactive figure.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH2 - Sitting room night (Scene 4): Aberforth's account of Ariana and Albus
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus (Scenes 143–186) establishes Aberforth delivering an extended, emotionally devastating first-person account of Ariana's suffering, his own role as her primary caretaker ('I was her favourite… I could get her to eat when she wouldn't do it for my mother'), his confrontation with Grindelwald and Albus, the three-way duel, and Ariana's death. This monologue is the cornerstone of Aberforth's characterisation: a man of deep, inarticulate love, long-suppressed grief, and specific moral authority over his brother's failures.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film (Scene 4) entirely omits Aberforth's personal narrative. He does not describe Ariana's attack by Muggle boys, his role as her carer, his confrontation with Grindelwald, the duel, or Ariana's death. Instead he offers only a compressed, abstract charge: 'My brother sacrificed many things, Mr. Potter, in his journey to find power, including her. She was devoted to him — he gave her everything, but time.' This reduces a detailed, emotionally specific monologue to a single vague line of grievance.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The monologue is the only moment in the entire saga where Aberforth is given full dramatic agency to speak in his own voice about his own life. Its removal strips him of his defining characterisation — the grieving, fiercely loving brother — and replaces it with a generic antagonist pose. It also removes the audience's understanding of exactly what Albus sacrificed and why Aberforth's bitterness is justified, degrading the moral complexity of Dumbledore's arc.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH2 - Sitting room night (Scene 4): Aberforth's role as Ariana's primary caretaker
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus (Scenes 152–157) establishes that Aberforth — not Albus — was Ariana's favoured caretaker. He could get her to eat, calm her rages, and she helped him feed the goats. This detail is the emotional heart of his character: his bond with her is particular, tender, and earned through daily care.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film reverses this. Aberforth says Ariana 'was devoted to him [Albus]' and that Albus 'gave her everything, but time.' This frames the Albus–Ariana bond as the central one and erases Aberforth's unique relationship with her entirely.
damaging_scenes.explanation: By attributing Ariana's devotion to Albus rather than Aberforth, the film undermines the very reason Aberforth's grief carries moral weight. His anger at Albus is rooted in the fact that he — not Albus — was her carer, and Albus's distraction with Grindelwald was a betrayal of a specific, intimate family responsibility. The film's inversion makes Aberforth's grievance less legible and his relationship with Ariana nearly invisible.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH2 - Sitting room night (Scene 4): Aberforth's confrontation of Grindelwald and Albus
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus (Scenes 170–179) establishes that the teenage Aberforth directly confronted both Albus and Grindelwald, told them to abandon their plans, and pulled his wand when Grindelwald cursed him — showing him as physically brave, morally clear-sighted, and willing to act even against his more powerful brother and his friend.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This confrontation is entirely absent from the film corpus. No version of this scene appears in the theatrical material provided.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The confrontation is the one moment in the books where Aberforth exercises clear moral agency, standing up to two more powerful wizards on behalf of his vulnerable sister. Its absence means the film Aberforth has no demonstrated heroism or courage in his backstory — only bitterness and resignation. This flattens him from a morally active figure into a passive one.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH2 - Sitting room night (Scene 4): Aberforth's challenge to Harry and his eventual yielding
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus (Scenes 95–210) shows a prolonged, multi-beat exchange in which Aberforth argues strenuously that the war is lost and Harry should flee, Harry pushes back, and Aberforth's resistance is worn down until he finally — without explicit capitulation — gets up and activates the portrait. The book also includes Harry invoking Dumbledore's dying vision (Scenes 191–193), a moment that visibly affects Aberforth and shifts the dynamic.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film (Scene 4) condenses this exchange significantly. Harry's invocation of Dumbledore's final tormented visions ('He thought he was back there with you and Grindelwald') is absent. Aberforth's yielding comes after Harry's declaration of faith in Dumbledore, but the specific emotional lever — Harry telling Aberforth that his brother died in anguish over Ariana — is cut.
damaging_scenes.explanation: In the book, Aberforth is moved partly by the revelation that Albus was not free of guilt even at death — that he still suffered over Ariana. This gives Aberforth's decision to help a richer motivation: not just grudging pragmatism but a partial reconciliation with his brother's memory. The film's version makes his yield feel more like defeat than resolution, weakening the emotional arc of the scene.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH2 - Sitting room night (Scene 4): Film insult to Harry ('You're lying… That's what a fool does')
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus (Scenes 95–136) shows Aberforth challenging Harry sharply but never accusing him of lying or calling him a fool. Aberforth's critique is directed at Albus ('Secrets and lies, that's how we grew up') and at the danger of blind trust, not at Harry's personal integrity.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film (Scene 4) has Aberforth tell Harry directly: 'You're lying. Not just to me, which doesn't matter, but to yourself as well. That's what a fool does.' This is a direct personal attack on Harry's honesty and intelligence not present in the book exchange.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While Aberforth is blunt and cynical in both versions, the book's version directs his bitterness at Albus and at circumstance, not at Harry personally. The film's phrasing makes him more gratuitously hostile toward Harry, slightly distorting his voice from 'grieving realist' toward 'antagonist,' and weakens the sense that he ultimately respects and protects Harry.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH2 - Sitting room night (Scene 4): Aberforth's description of Ariana's condition and their father's sacrifice
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus (Scenes 145–151) establishes that Ariana was attacked by Muggle boys who saw her doing magic and tried to stop her doing it again, that the trauma broke something in her, and that their father went to Azkaban rather than reveal why he attacked those boys — protecting Ariana at the cost of his own freedom. This backstory humanises the entire Dumbledore family.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: None of this backstory appears in the film corpus. The film version of Aberforth provides no account of Ariana's attack, her condition, or Percival Dumbledore's sacrifice.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Without this material, the film audience has no understanding of why Ariana was hidden, what her condition actually was, or the family's pattern of self-sacrifice and secrecy. Aberforth's grief and anger lack the specific grounding that makes them comprehensible rather than merely bitter. The father's sacrifice — a direct parallel to Harry's own situation — is entirely lost.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH2 - Sitting room night (Scene 4): Aberforth's self-identification as the brother who stayed
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus (Scene 164–166) has Aberforth explicitly state: 'I'd have looked after her, I told him so, I didn't care about school, I'd have stayed home and done it.' This positions him as the responsible sibling who offered sacrifice and was overruled, not merely a resentful outsider.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This declaration is absent from the film. The film Aberforth voices grievance but never articulates what he was willing to do or what was taken from him.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The absence of this line means the film Aberforth appears to criticise without having offered an alternative. In the book, his moral authority comes precisely from his willingness to sacrifice his own education and ambitions for Ariana. Without it, his critique of Albus reads as jealousy rather than earned grievance.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH2 - Battle of Hogwarts (Scene 7 / post-battle Great Hall): Aberforth's role in the battle
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus (Scenes 231–246) shows Aberforth actively fighting in the Battle of Hogwarts: blocking corridors, leading students, offering tactical commentary (north battlements, giants), and personally Stunning Rookwood. He is a combatant, not merely a bystander.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's post-battle scene (Scene 7) shows Aberforth sitting with Oliver Wood drinking something strong and giving Harry 'a stoic nod.' No fighting is depicted or referenced.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While the film does show him present in the aftermath, his active participation in the battle — which in the book is the payoff for his earlier reluctance, showing he did not in fact give up — is entirely invisible. The 'stoic nod' reads as passive rather than as the concluding beat of a character arc from cynicism to action.
